To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the epidermal-growth-factor receptor (EGFR) maintains the intracellular glucose level and prevents autophagic cell-death in cancer cells.

the kinase activity of the EGFR is dispensable to maintain cancer cells, and that the kinase-independent EGFR maintains cancer cells by preventing cell death through the stabilization of a glucose transporter.
EGFR, independent of its kinase function, maintains intracellular glucose level in cancer cells by interaction with SGLT1.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the kinase-independent function of EGFR in cancer cells and the potential of targeting this function for cancer therapy.

the identification of a novel mechanism by which EGFR maintains cancer cell survival and provides a rationale for the combination therapy of SGLT1 inhibitor and EGFR kinase inhibitor for cancer treatment.
the role of EGFR in cancer cell survival and the potential therapeutic implications.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
SGLT1 is an essential factor for EGFR to maintain intracellular glucose level, which prevents autophagic cell deaths in cancer cells, and this function is independent of the kinase activity.
SGLT1 expression is a key determinant of EGFR function, and EGFR is a key regulator of SGLT1.
EGFR maintains intracellular glucose level and prevents autophagic cell by stabilizing SGLT1.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the EGFR-SGLT1 complex is required for cancer cells to maintain intracellular glucose level for autophagic cell survival, and this function is independent of EGFR kinase activity.
EGFR is a glucose sensor in human cancer cells.
in the absence of EGFR kinase activity, EGFR maintains the survival of cancer cells by stabilizing SGLT1.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the EGFR/SGLT1 axis can be a novel target for cancer therapy.
EGFR can be a potential therapeutic target for cancer treatment by targeting its interaction with SGLT1.
the function of EGFR is not only kinase-dependent, but also kinase-independent, and that the latter is critical to maintain the survival of cancer cells.
